subject: Design choice: east-west access for SageHealth private deployment — recommendation and fallback plan

Subject: SageHealth private deployment — path selection (peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S)

Hi team,

Thanks again for the walkthrough today. To summarize our constraints and primary asks: 
- We need Redwood Private deployed in our AWS account to serve on-prem inference requests from multiple hospital sites (latency target: <= 50ms internal regional);
- Data is PHI — strict egress audit + non-public network only;
- Some sites are already backhauled to our AWS VPCs via site-to-site VPNs (IPsec) and we may expand to direct cross-account VPC peering in future;
- We prefer the minimal operational lift for our network team — but willing to accept some setup for better performance/security.

Specific ask: recommend a preferred connectivity pattern (VPC Peering vs AWS PrivateLink vs S2S VPN) for control plane and data plane, and provide a fallback plan and a short implementation checklist. Any obvious blockers we should know about (route table limits, transitive routes, DNS, certs)?

Attaching a very small network diagram and our current VPN termination sheet.

Best,
Aaron (SageHealth DevOps)

Attachments: sagemap-highlevel-diagram.pdf (diagram), current-vpn-terminations.csv (list)

Subject: Re: SageHealth private deployment — path selection (peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S)

Aaron — thanks for the clear summary and diagram. High level: 3 patterns are all viable but they have different operational/security trade-offs. I pulled the team in to create a concise recommendation + checklist (see attached later). Below is a quick executive summary so we can align on risk appetite before we produce the detailed config.

Executive summary (short):
- Recommended primary: AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for the Redwood control/API plane and metadata (authentication, billing, routing).
- Recommended data path: Use VPC Peering inside AWS for high-throughput bulk inference traffic when the compute and customer VPCs are in the same region/account boundary where peering is supported.
- Secondary/fallback: S2S VPN for on-prem sites that cannot be re-architected quickly — use for legacy sites and DR only.

Rationale in one line: PrivateLink gives tight surface-area (no public IPs or route propagation) and better inbound access control; peering wins for raw throughput and lower per-packet latency inside cloud; vendor-managed S2S is easy to set up for on-prem but has higher operational latency variability and weaker isolation for multi-tenant cloud designs.

I'll let Kimberly and Marcus add operational detail (route table scale, ENI limits, observability hooks) and Karthik will add the code snippets for endpoint policies and mutual TLS requirements.

— Hannah

Subject: Re: SageHealth private deployment — path selection (peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S)

Aaron / team — expanding Hannah's summary into operational trade-offs and a short checklist you can action. I kept this high-signal and included the things customers most trip on.

Option comparisons (short bullets):
- AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoint)
  - Pros: No route table changes required in consumer VPCs, traffic never traverses public internet, each endpoint is an ENI + private IP in consumer subnets; integrates well with Private DNS for endpoint hostnames; supports granular endpoint policies so you can lock to specific service principals.
  - Cons: ENI limits per AZ (watch if you need many endpoints + AZs), per-GB costs for data processed by interface endpoints (govern billing), cross-account conditions require correct IAM principals, and you still need to manage NLBs or service network load balancers in the provider VPC.

- VPC Peering
  - Pros: Lowest latency and no per-packet interface endpoint cost; transparent routing (for same-region), great for high-throughput, and simpler for intra-cloud data plane where both VPCs are under your control.
  - Cons: No transitive routing (peers don't transit), requires route table entries and careful CIDR planning to avoid overlap, cross-account peering is supported but operationally more complex for many partners. Peering can become a sprawl problem if you have dozens of customer VPCs.

- Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec)
  - Pros: Works with existing on-prem hardware, encrypted link out-of-the-box, good for legacy foot-prints; easy to stand up for testing/POC.
  - Cons: Variable latency, throughput limited by on-prem devices, increased operational churn (rekeying, monitoring), and harder to meet strict SLOs for latency-sensitive inference.

Recommended hybrid pattern (what we propose):
1) PrivateLink for the Redwood control plane and authentication endpoints (token exchange, config). This limits the attack surface and centralizes auth flows through interface endpoints.
2) VPC Peering for the data plane when SageHealth compute and Redwood inference pools are colocated in the same cloud account/region — use AWS ENIs and colocated batch sizing for higher throughput and <50ms internal latency.
3) Maintain S2S VPNs as a managed fallback for hospital sites that cannot move traffic to the cloud path quickly; treat these links as best-effort and limit high-volume inference jobs across VPN.

Operational checklist (short):
- Confirm CIDR non-overlap for any VPC peering (run CIDR audit).
- Estimate ENI count: PrivateLink endpoints per AZ + service side NLB targets.
- Benchmark egress costs (PrivateLink vs Peering).
- Decide private DNS strategy: private hosted zone pointing to endpoint IPs vs conditional forwarding.
- Set endpoint policies: restrict to service principals and approve only Redwood service accounts.
- Prepare flow logs + VPC flow collector for traffic auditing (PHI).
- mTLS + short-lived certs for service-to-service auth; store root in your KMS/HSM and configure rotation.

Attachments included: a checklist spreadsheet (privatelink-vs-peering-checklist.xlsx) and a sample parameter file for PrivateLink (aws-privatelink-sample-params.txt). We'll populate example CloudFormation snippets once you confirm the pattern.

If you want, Marcus and I can produce a small pilot plan for an initial peering + PrivateLink combination in one test region and run a 72-hour SLA soak test.

— Kimberly
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Adding a few production-operational notes and a canary plan.

Operational notes / gotchas:
- ENI and IP exhaustion: when using PrivateLink across many subnets/AZs, track per-AZ ENI limits and reserve IP pools; we normally ask customers to reserve a /24 per AZ for service endpoints to avoid surprises.
- Route table churn: peering requires explicit route table updates for each subnet; for large-scale multi-VPC installs we prefer to automate route rollouts via IaC (Terraform) and tag-based validations.
- Cross-account peering permissions: ensure both accounts accept peering and check AWS RAM if you plan to share resources.
- Flow logs + SIEM: push VPC flow logs to centralized S3 + Athena and also to your SIEM for PHI egress alerts. Set alert thresholds for traffic leaving PrivateLink endpoints unexpectedly.

Canary execution plan (3 phases):
1) Phase 1 (pilot): Deploy Redwood Private in a test VPC in us-east-1. Create PrivateLink endpoint for control plane only. Create a peering link between test VPC and your dev VPC. Run synthetic inference traffic (10k req/day) and capture p50/p95 latency and packet drop.
2) Phase 2 (expanded pilot): Add one hospital site over S2S VPN and route only metadata/auth traffic via PrivateLink; route payload via peering. Run mixed production-like traffic for 72 hours; validate PHI audit logs.
3) Phase 3 (rollout): If P95/latency and audit look good, expand peering connections for other in-cloud sites and migrate additional hospitals off VPN gradually.

Fallbacks: If we observe packet loss or latency spikes on peering, we can shift traffic to PrivateLink-backed NLBs (smaller payload chunks) or fall back to hosted Redwood API for a short window while we troubleshoot network. We'll instrument switches with feature flags.

Operational deliverables we will provide: IaC snippets for peering + endpoint creation, an alerting playbook (runbook) for NAT/ENI exhaustion, and a small runbook for VPN rekey and reestablishing routes.

— Marcus
Senior Network Engineer, Redwood Inference
